text: PROJECT REPORT With the inlet CO concentration now calculated from Calpine data, ION moved the Horiba 2 sampling point to the outlet flue gas. The CO concentration in the outlet flue gas was then 2 measured and stored using the Horiba CO analyzer. 2 Moving the Horiba to the outlet flue gas allowed ION to have continuous, reliable CO concentration data for both the inlet and outlet flue gas streams. 2 ION also replaced the Gasmet FTIR, which was not sensitive enough to measure ppb-levels of emissions. To that end, ION PTR-TOF mass spectrometer. Flue gas outlet emissions of ammonia, formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and VOCs in the outlet flue gas were then measured using the PTR- TOF. The PTR-TOF can measure individual components down to below the parts-per-billion (ppb) level. 8.3 Solvent Analysis Solvent samples were shipped from ENTP to ION’s laboratory in Boulder, CO. Samples of the rich and lean solvent were taken twice a day at 12-hour increments (one early morning sample and one afternoon sample). Samples were refrigerated until shipment and again refrigerated in ION’s laboratory. Solvent water content was measured using Karl-Fischer titration. CO loading was 2 measured using total inorganic carbon (TIC) analysis, main solvent components were measured using gas chromatography with mass spectrometry (GC-MS), and trace heat stable salts were measured using ion chromatography (IC). All measurements were performed in triplicate to ensure precise analysis and demonstrate high reproducibility. 8.4 Specific Reboiler Duty Specific Reboiler Duty (heat input per unit of CO captured) is calculated based on the condensate 2 flow rate out of the reboiler. ION chose to use the condensate flow rate instead of the steam flow rate since the condensate flowmeter can be externally calibrated gravimetrically. The calibration utilized 140 °F water in the condensate tank and at various valve positions that matched the normal operating range of the condensate flowmeter (Figure 8-2) ION found the flowmeter to be very accurate in the operating range, with the flow calculated from the scale about 1.5% higher than the flowmeter readings. However, since the calibration was done at 140 °F instead of the normal operating temperature of 210 °F, the operating flow needed to be corrected for temperature. To do this, ION defined the flow determined from the scale reading (the true flow) as proportional to the flowmeter reading (which is analogous to the velocity being measured by the flowmeter). ION then defined the proportionality constant as the product of the density of the stream and some constant k, where the proportionality constant is equal to the slope of the line created when graphing scale flow versus actual flow (which is where the 1.5% comes from). Using this relationship, the true flow at 210 °F is thus equal to the ratio of density at 210 °F and 140 °F times the flowmeter reading times 1.5%.
